{{short description|Formula for the derivative of a product}}
{{about|the derivative of a product|the relation between derivatives of 3 dependent variables|Triple product rule|a counting principle in combinatorics|Rule of product|conditional probabilities|Chain rule (probability)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2022}}
[[File:Schema_Règle_produit.png|thumb|300px|right|Geometric illustration of a proof of the product rule<ref>Note: This is a usual image since the 17th century, essentially the same illustration given in [[James Stewart (mathematician)|James Stewart]]: ''Calculus: Early Transcendentals'' edition 7, p. 185 in the section "The geometry of the Product Rule".</ref>]]
{{Calculus |Differential}}

In [[calculus]], the '''product rule''' (or '''Leibniz rule'''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Leibniz_rule|title=Leibniz rule – Encyclopedia of Mathematics}}</ref> or '''Leibniz product rule''') is a formula used to find the [[derivative]]s of products of two or more [[Functions (mathematics)|functions]]. For two functions, it may be stated in [[Notation for differentiation#Lagrange's notation|Lagrange's notation]] as <math display="block">(u \cdot v)' = u ' \cdot v + u \cdot v' </math> or in [[Leibniz's notation]] as <math display="block">\frac{d}{dx} (u\cdot v) = \frac{du}{dx} \cdot v + u \cdot \frac{dv}{dx}.</math>

The rule may be extended or generalized to products of three or more functions, to a rule for higher-order derivatives of a product, and to other contexts.

== Discovery ==
Discovery of this rule is credited to [[Gottfried Leibniz]], who demonstrated it using [[Nonstandard_calculus#Motivation|"infinitesimals"]] (a precursor to the modern [[differential (calculus)|differential]]).<ref>{{cite journal |author=Michelle Cirillo |journal=The Mathematics Teacher |volume=101 |issue=1 |pages=23–27 |date=August 2007 |title=Humanizing Calculus | doi = 10.5951/MT.101.1.0023 |url=http://www.nctm.org/publications/article.aspx?id=19302 | url-access = subscription }}</ref> (However, J. M. Child, a translator of Leibniz's papers,<ref>{{citation|first=G. W.|last=Leibniz|url=https://dynref.engr.illinois.edu/rvc_Child_1920.pdf|title= The Early Mathematical Manuscripts of Leibniz|translator=J.M. Child|year=2005|orig-year=1920|publisher=Dover|page= 28, footnote 58|isbn=978-0-486-44596-0}}</ref> argues that it is due to [[Isaac Barrow]].) Here is Leibniz's argument:<ref>{{citation|first=G. W.|last=Leibniz|url=https://dynref.engr.illinois.edu/rvc_Child_1920.pdf|title= The Early Mathematical Manuscripts of Leibniz|translator=J.M. Child|year=2005|orig-year=1920|publisher=Dover|page=143|isbn=978-0-486-44596-0}}</ref> Let ''u'' and ''v'' be functions. Then ''d(uv)'' is the same thing as the difference between two successive ''uv'''s; let one of these be ''uv'', and the other ''u+du'' times ''v+dv''; then:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
d(u\cdot v) & {} = (u + du)\cdot (v + dv) - u\cdot v \\
& {} = u\cdot dv + v\cdot du + du\cdot dv.
\end{align}</math>

Since the term ''du''·''dv'' is "negligible" (compared to ''du'' and ''dv''), Leibniz concluded that
<math display="block">d(u\cdot v) = v\cdot du + u\cdot dv </math>
and this is indeed the differential form of the product rule. If we divide through by the differential ''dx'', we obtain
<math display="block">\frac{d}{dx} (u\cdot v) = v \cdot \frac{du}{dx} + u \cdot  \frac{dv}{dx} </math>
which can also be written in [[Derivative#Lagrange.27s notation|Lagrange's notation]] as
<math display="block">(u\cdot v)' = v\cdot  u' + u\cdot  v'. </math>

===First proofs===

Both Leibniz and [[Isaac Newton|Newton]] gave [[Mathematical proof|proof]]s that are not [[Mathematical rigor|rigorous]] by modern standards. Leibniz reasoned with "[[Infinitesimal|infinitely smaller quantities]]", interpreting products as [[area]]s of [[rectangle]]s, while Newton reasoned with "[[Fluxion|flowing quantities]]".<ref>Eugene Boman, and Robert Rogers. ''Real Analysis'' https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Analysis/Real_Analysis_(Boman_and_Rogers)/02%3A_Calculus_in_the_17th_and_18th_Centuries/2.01%3A_Newton_and_Leibniz_Get_Started</ref><ref>{{Cite web| title=A Story of Real Analysis | url=https://milneopentextbooks.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/12/A_Story_of_Real_Analysis_ebook-pdf.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250311041001/https://milneopentextbooks.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/12/A_Story_of_Real_Analysis_ebook-pdf.pdf | archive-date=2025-03-11}}</ref>

== Examples ==
*Suppose we want to differentiate <math>f(x)=x^2\text {sin}(x).</math> By using the product rule, one gets the derivative <math>f'(x)=2x\cdot \text {sin}(x)+x^2\text {cos} (x)</math> (since the derivative of <math>x^2</math> is <math>2x,</math> and the derivative of the [[sine]] function is the cosine function).
*One special case of the product rule is the [[constant multiple rule]], which states: if {{mvar|c}} is a number, and <math>f(x)</math> is a differentiable function, then <math>c\cdot f(x)</math> is also differentiable, and its derivative is <math>(cf)'(x)=c \cdot f'(x).</math> This follows from the product rule since the derivative of any constant is zero. This, combined with the sum rule for derivatives, shows that differentiation is [[linear transformation|linear]].
*The rule for [[integration by parts]] is derived from the product rule, as is (a weak version of) the [[quotient rule]]. (It is a "weak" version in that it does not prove that the quotient is differentiable but only says what its derivative is {{em|if}} it is differentiable.)

== Proofs ==

=== Limit definition of derivative ===

Let {{math|''h''(''x'') {{=}} ''f''(''x'')''g''(''x'')}} and suppose that {{mvar|f}} and {{mvar|g}} are each differentiable at {{mvar|x}}. We want to prove that {{mvar|h}} is differentiable at {{mvar|x}} and that its derivative, {{math|''{{prime|h}}''(''x'')}}, is given by {{math|''{{prime|f}}''(''x'')''g''(''x'') + ''f''(''x'')''{{prime|g}}''(''x'')}}. To do this, <math>f(x)g(x+\Delta x)-f(x)g(x+\Delta x)</math> (which is zero, and thus does not change the value) is added to the numerator to permit its factoring, and then properties of limits are used.
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 h'(x) &= \lim_{\Delta x\to 0} \frac{h(x+\Delta x)-h(x)}{\Delta x} \\[5pt]
   &= \lim_{\Delta x\to 0} \frac{f(x+\Delta x)g(x+\Delta x)-f(x)g(x)}{\Delta x} \\[5pt]
   &= \lim_{\Delta x\to 0} \frac{f(x+\Delta x)g(x+\Delta x)-f(x)g(x+\Delta x)+f(x)g(x+\Delta x)-f(x)g(x)}{\Delta x} \\[5pt]
   &= \lim_{\Delta x\to 0} \frac{\big[f(x+\Delta x)-f(x)\big] \cdot g(x+\Delta x) + f(x) \cdot \big[g(x+\Delta x)-g(x)\big]}{\Delta x} \\[5pt]
   &= \lim_{\Delta x\to 0} \frac{f(x+\Delta x)-f(x)}{\Delta x} \cdot \lim_{\Delta x\to 0} g(x+\Delta x)
     + \lim_{\Delta x\to 0} f(x) \cdot \lim_{\Delta x\to 0} \frac{g(x+\Delta x)-g(x)}{\Delta x} \\[5pt]
   &= f'(x)g(x)+f(x)g'(x).
\end{align}</math>
The fact that <math> \lim_{\Delta x\to0} g(x+\Delta x) = g(x) </math> follows from the fact that differentiable functions are continuous.

=== Linear approximations ===
By definition, if <math> f, g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} </math> are differentiable at <math> x </math>, then we can write [[Linear approximation|linear approximations]]:
<math display="block"> f(x+h) = f(x) + f'(x)h + \varepsilon_1(h) </math> and <math display="block"> g(x+h) = g(x) + g'(x)h + \varepsilon_2(h), </math>
where the error terms are small with respect to ''h'': that is, <math display="inline"> \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\varepsilon_1(h)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\varepsilon_2(h)}{h} = 0, </math> [[Big O notation#Little-o notation|also written]] <math>\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2 \sim o(h)</math>. Then:
<math display="block"> \begin{align} 
   f(x+h)g(x+h) - f(x)g(x) &=  (f(x) + f'(x)h +\varepsilon_1(h))(g(x) + g'(x)h + \varepsilon_2(h)) - f(x)g(x) \\[.5em]
                   &= f(x)g(x) + f'(x)g(x)h + f(x)g'(x)h -f(x)g(x) + \text{error terms} \\[.5em]
                   &= f'(x)g(x)h + f(x)g'(x)h + o(h) . 
\end{align} </math>
The "error terms" consist of items such as <math>f(x)\varepsilon_2(h), f'(x)g'(x)h^2</math> and <math>hf'(x)\varepsilon_1(h)</math> which are easily seen to have magnitude <math>o(h).</math> Dividing by <math> h </math> and taking the limit <math> h\to 0 </math> gives the result.

=== Quarter squares ===
This proof uses the [[chain rule]] and the [[Multiplication algorithm#Quarter square multiplication|quarter square function]] <math>q(x)=\tfrac14x^2</math> with derivative <math>q'(x) = \tfrac12 x</math>. We have:
<math display="block">uv=q(u+v)-q(u-v), </math>
and differentiating both sides gives:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
f' &= q'(u+v)(u'+v') - q'(u-v)(u'-v') \\[4pt]
&= \left(\tfrac12(u+v)(u'+v')\right) - \left(\tfrac12(u-v)(u'-v')\right) \\[4pt]
&= \tfrac12(uu' + vu' + uv' + vv') - \tfrac12(uu' - vu' - uv' + vv') \\[4pt]
&= vu'+uv' .
\end{align}</math>

=== Multivariable chain rule ===
The product rule can be considered a special case of the [[chain rule]] for several variables, applied to the multiplication function <math>m(u,v) = uv</math>:
<math display="block"> {d (uv) \over dx} = \frac{\partial(uv)}{\partial u}\frac{du}{dx}+\frac{\partial (uv)}{\partial v}\frac{dv}{dx} = v \frac{du}{dx} + u \frac{dv}{dx}. </math>

=== Non-standard analysis ===
Let ''u'' and ''v'' be continuous functions in ''x'', and let ''dx'', ''du'' and ''dv'' be [[infinitesimal]]s within the framework of [[non-standard analysis]], specifically the [[hyperreal number]]s. Using st to denote the [[standard part function]] that associates to a [[wiktionary:Finite number|finite]] hyperreal number the real infinitely close to it, this gives
<math display="block">\begin{align}
   \frac{d(uv)}{dx} &= \operatorname{st}\left(\frac{(u + du)(v + dv) - uv}{dx}\right) \\
   &= \operatorname{st}\left(\frac{uv + u \cdot dv + v \cdot du + du \cdot dv -uv}{dx}\right) \\
   &= \operatorname{st}\left(\frac{u \cdot dv + v \cdot du + du \cdot dv}{dx}\right) \\
   &= \operatorname{st}\left(u \frac{dv}{dx} + (v + dv) \frac{du}{dx}\right) \\
   &= u \frac{dv}{dx} + v \frac{du}{dx}.
 \end{align}</math>
This was essentially [[Leibniz]]'s proof exploiting the [[transcendental law of homogeneity]] (in place of the standard part above).

===Smooth infinitesimal analysis===
In the context of Lawvere's approach to infinitesimals, let <math>dx</math> be a nilsquare infinitesimal. Then <math>du = u'\ dx</math> and <math>dv = v'\ dx</math>, so that
<math display="block">\begin{align}
d(uv) & = (u + du)(v + dv)  -uv \\
 & = uv + u \cdot dv + v \cdot du + du \cdot dv - uv \\
 & = u \cdot dv + v \cdot du + du \cdot dv \\
 & = u \cdot dv + v \cdot du
\end{align}</math>
since <math>du \, dv = u' v' (dx)^2 = 0.</math> Dividing by <math>dx</math> then gives <math>\frac{d(uv)}{dx} = u \frac{dv}{dx} + v \frac{du}{dx}</math> or <math>(uv)' = u \cdot v' + v \cdot u'</math>.

===Logarithmic differentiation===

Let <math>h(x) = f(x) g(x)</math>. Taking the [[absolute value]] of each function and the [[Natural logarithm|natural log]] of both sides of the equation, 
<math display="block">\ln|h(x)| = \ln|f(x) g(x)| </math>
Applying properties of the absolute value and logarithms, 
<math display="block">\ln|h(x)| = \ln|f(x)| + \ln|g(x)| </math> 
Taking the [[logarithmic derivative]] of both sides and then solving for <math>h'(x) </math>:
<math display="block">\frac{h'(x)}{h(x)} = \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} + \frac{g'(x)}{g(x)}</math>
Solving for <math>h'(x)</math> and substituting back <math>f(x) g(x)</math> for <math>h(x)</math> gives:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
h'(x) &= h(x)\left(\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} + \frac{g'(x)}{g(x)}\right) \\
&= f(x) g(x)\left(\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} + \frac{g'(x)}{g(x)}\right) \\
&= f'(x) g(x) + f(x) g'(x).
\end{align}</math>
Note: Taking the absolute value of the functions is necessary for the [[logarithmic differentiation]] of functions that may have negative values, as logarithms are only [[Real-valued function|real-valued]] for positive arguments. This works because <math>\tfrac{d}{dx}(\ln |u|) = \tfrac{u'}{u}</math>, which justifies taking the absolute value of the functions for logarithmic differentiation.

== Generalizations ==
=== Product of more than two factors ===
The product rule can be generalized to products of more than two factors. For example, for three factors we have
<math display="block">\frac{d(uvw)}{dx} = \frac{du}{dx}vw + u\frac{dv}{dx}w + uv\frac{dw}{dx}.</math>
For a collection of functions <math>f_1, \dots, f_k</math>, we have
<math display="block">\frac{d}{dx} \left [ \prod_{i=1}^k f_i(x) \right ]
 = \sum_{i=1}^k \left(\left(\frac{d}{dx} f_i(x) \right) \prod_{j=1,j\ne i}^k f_j(x) \right)
= \left(  \prod_{i=1}^k f_i(x) \right) \left( \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{f'_i(x)}{f_i(x)} \right).</math>

The [[logarithmic derivative]] provides a simpler expression of the last form, as well as a direct proof that does not involve any [[recursion]]. The ''logarithmic derivative''   of a function {{mvar|f}}, denoted here {{math|Logder(''f'')}}, is the derivative of the [[logarithm]] of the function. It follows that 
<math display="block">\operatorname{Logder}(f)=\frac {f'}f.</math>
Using that the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms of the factors, the [[sum rule in differentiation|sum rule]] for derivatives gives immediately
<math display="block">\operatorname{Logder}(f_1\cdots f_k)= \sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{Logder}(f_i).</math>
The last above expression of the derivative of a product is obtained by multiplying both members of this equation by the product of the <math>f_i.</math>

=== Higher derivatives ===
{{Main|General Leibniz rule}}
It can also be generalized to the [[general Leibniz rule]] for the ''n''th derivative of a product of two factors, by symbolically expanding according to the [[binomial theorem]]:
<math display="block">d^n(uv) = \sum_{k=0}^n {n \choose k} \cdot d^{(n-k)}(u)\cdot  d^{(k)}(v).</math>

Applied at a specific point ''x'', the above formula gives: 
<math display="block">(uv)^{(n)}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n {n \choose k} \cdot u^{(n-k)}(x)\cdot  v^{(k)}(x).</math>

Furthermore, for the ''n''th derivative of an arbitrary number of factors, one has a similar formula with [[Multinomial theorem|multinomial coefficients]]:
<math display="block">\left(\prod_{i=1}^kf_i\right)^{\!\!(n)}=\sum_{j_1+j_2+\cdots+j_k=n}{n\choose j_1,j_2,\ldots,j_k}\prod_{i=1}^kf_i^{(j_i)}.</math>

=== Higher partial derivatives ===
For [[partial derivative]]s, we have<ref>{{cite journal |author=Michael Hardy | journal=The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics |volume=13 |date=January 2006 |title=Combinatorics of Partial Derivatives | arxiv = math/0601149 |bibcode = 2006math......1149H |url=https://www.emis.de//journals/EJC/Volume_13/PDF/v13i1r1.pdf }}</ref>
<math display="block">{\partial^n \over \partial x_1\,\cdots\,\partial x_n} (uv)
= \sum_S {\partial^{|S|} u \over \prod_{i\in S} \partial x_i} \cdot {\partial^{n-|S|} v \over \prod_{i\not\in S} \partial x_i}</math>
where the index {{mvar|S}} runs through all {{math|2<sup>''n''</sup>}} [[subset]]s of {{math|{{mset|1, ..., ''n''}}}}, and {{math|{{mabs|''S''}}}} is the [[cardinality]] of {{mvar|S}}. For example, when {{math|1=''n'' = 3}},
<math display="block">\begin{align} & {\partial^3 \over \partial x_1\,\partial x_2\,\partial x_3} (uv)  \\[1ex]
= {} & u \cdot{\partial^3 v \over \partial x_1\,\partial x_2\,\partial x_3} + {\partial u \over \partial x_1}\cdot{\partial^2 v \over \partial x_2\,\partial x_3} +  {\partial u \over \partial x_2}\cdot{\partial^2 v \over \partial x_1\,\partial x_3} + {\partial u \over \partial x_3}\cdot{\partial^2 v \over \partial x_1\,\partial x_2} \\[1ex]
&  + {\partial^2 u \over \partial x_1\,\partial x_2}\cdot{\partial v \over \partial x_3}
+ {\partial^2 u \over \partial x_1\,\partial x_3}\cdot{\partial v \over \partial x_2}
+ {\partial^2 u \over \partial x_2\,\partial x_3}\cdot{\partial v \over \partial x_1}
+ {\partial^3 u \over \partial x_1\,\partial x_2\,\partial x_3}\cdot v. \\[-3ex]&\end{align}</math>

=== Banach space ===
Suppose ''X'', ''Y'', and ''Z'' are [[Banach space]]s (which includes [[Euclidean space]]) and ''B'' : ''X'' &times; ''Y'' → ''Z'' is a [[continuous function (topology)|continuous]] [[bilinear operator]]. Then ''B'' is differentiable, and its derivative at the point (''x'',''y'') in ''X'' &times; ''Y'' is the [[linear map]] ''D''<sub>(''x'',''y'')</sub>''B'' : ''X'' &times; ''Y'' → ''Z'' given by
<math display="block"> (D_\left( x,y \right)\,B)\left( u,v \right) = B\left( u,y \right) + B\left( x,v \right)\qquad\forall (u,v)\in X \times Y. </math>

This result can be extended<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kreigl |first1=Andreas |last2=Michor |first2=Peter |title=The Convenient Setting of Global Analysis |date=1997 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |isbn=0-8218-0780-3 |page=59 |url=https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~michor/apbookh-ams.pdf}}</ref> to more general topological vector spaces.

=== In vector calculus ===
{{Main|Vector calculus identities#First derivative identities}}

The product rule extends to various product operations of vector functions on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>:<ref>{{citation|last = Stewart | first = James|title = Calculus | edition = 8 | publisher = Cengage|year = 2016}}, Section 13.2.</ref>

* For [[scalar multiplication]]: <math display="block">(f \cdot \mathbf g)' = f'\cdot \mathbf g + f \cdot \mathbf g' </math>
* For [[dot product]]: <math display="block">(\mathbf f \cdot \mathbf g)' = \mathbf f' \cdot \mathbf g + \mathbf f \cdot \mathbf g' </math>
* For [[cross product]] of vector functions on <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math>: <math display="block">(\mathbf f \times \mathbf g)' = \mathbf f' \times \mathbf g + \mathbf f \times \mathbf g' </math>

There are also analogues for other analogs of the derivative: if ''f'' and ''g'' are scalar fields then there is a product rule with the [[gradient]]:
<math display="block">\nabla (f \cdot g) = \nabla f \cdot g + f \cdot \nabla g </math>

Such a rule will hold for any continuous [[bilinear map|bilinear]] product operation.  Let ''B'' : ''X'' &times; ''Y'' → ''Z'' be a continuous bilinear map between vector spaces, and let ''f'' and ''g'' be differentiable functions into ''X'' and ''Y'', respectively.  The only properties of multiplication used in the proof using the [[#Limit definition of derivative|limit definition of derivative]] is that multiplication is continuous and bilinear.  So for any continuous bilinear operation,
<math display="block">H(f, g)' = H(f', g) + H(f, g').</math>
This is also a special case of the product rule for bilinear maps in [[#Banach space|Banach space]].

=== Derivations in abstract algebra and differential geometry ===
In [[abstract algebra]], the product rule is the defining property of a [[derivation (abstract algebra)|derivation]]. In this terminology, the product rule states that the derivative operator is a derivation  on functions. 

In [[differential geometry]], a [[tangent vector]] to a [[manifold]] ''M'' at a point ''p'' may be defined abstractly as an operator on real-valued functions which behaves like a [[directional derivative]] at ''p'': that is, a [[Linear form|linear functional]] ''v'' which is a derivation, <math display="block">v(fg) = v(f)\,g(p) + f(p) \, v(g).</math>
Generalizing (and dualizing) the formulas of vector calculus to an ''n''-dimensional manifold ''M,'' one may take [[Differential form|differential forms]] of degrees ''k'' and ''l'', denoted <math>\alpha\in \Omega^k(M), \beta\in \Omega^\ell(M)</math>, with the wedge or [[Exterior algebra|exterior product]] operation <math>\alpha\wedge\beta\in \Omega^{k+\ell}(M)</math>, as well as the [[exterior derivative]] <math>d:\Omega^m(M)\to\Omega^{m+1}(M)</math>. Then one has the [[Differential graded algebra|graded Leibniz rule]]: <math display="block">d(\alpha\wedge\beta)= d\alpha \wedge \beta + (-1)^{k} \alpha\wedge d\beta.</math>

== Applications ==
Among the applications of the product rule is a proof that
<math display="block"> {d \over dx} x^n = nx^{n-1}</math>
when ''n'' is a positive integer (this rule is true even if ''n'' is not positive or is not an integer, but the proof of that must rely on other methods). The proof is by [[mathematical induction]] on the exponent ''n''. If ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 then ''x''<sup>''n''</sup> is constant and ''nx''<sup>''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1</sup> = 0. The rule holds in that case because the derivative of a constant function is&nbsp;0. If the rule holds for any particular exponent ''n'', then for the next value, ''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1, we have
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{d x^{n+1}}{dx}
&{}= \frac{d}{dx} \left( x^n\cdot x\right) \\[1ex]
&{}= x \frac{d}{dx} x^n + x^n \frac{d}{dx} x & \text{(the product rule is used here)} \\[1ex]
&{}= x\left(n x^{n-1}\right) + x^n\cdot 1 & \text{(the induction hypothesis is used here)} \\[1ex]
&{}= \left(n + 1\right) x^n.
\end{align} </math>
Therefore, if the proposition is true for ''n'', it is true also for&nbsp;''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1, and therefore for all natural ''n''.
